idiom_name: final MonsterType class instance + static Map<String, MonsterType> registry
implementation_notes: java.lang.Class is the JVM's own type object and cannot carry domain fields, so the pattern is realized as an ordinary descriptor class shared by instances: final fields plus accessors, a package-private constructor called by the loader, and a static registry (immutable Map or ConcurrentHashMap) built from JSON/YAML at startup. Per-type behaviour is a functional interface (Function<Monster, String>, a small strategy enum, or a Strategy object) held on the descriptor. The descriptor's identity is its id - its equals is not the type identity. Use the class form on a Java 8 baseline or when descriptors need lazy fields; records (see variants) are the data-carrier alternative from Java 16 on. For a closed set of types an enum or sealed interface plus switch is simpler and exhaustive.
pitfalls: A static mutable HashMap registry is not thread-safe and leaks state across tests; build it once and publish an unmodifiable Map, or use ConcurrentHashMap.
Descriptors holding mutable collections (abilities, loot) are only shallowly immutable - wrap with List.copyOf/Map.copyOf at construction.
equals/hashCode on the descriptor (or on a record) makes two equal-looking descriptors interchangeable, so any Set/Map keyed by descriptor silently merges distinct types; key by id.

variants.name: Record descriptor (Java 16+)
variants.implementation_notes: A record is the language's explicit answer to 'modeling data as data': the header is the state, accessors/equals/hashCode/toString are derived, and components are final - so the descriptor becomes one declaration with no boilerplate and immutability is enforced by the compiler. The registry is built as a List<MonsterType> from the loader and indexed into an unmodifiable Map<String, MonsterType>; a factory method still lives next to the type (a static method on the record or a small factory class, since records cannot add instance state). Choose this variant when the toolchain is Java 16+ and descriptors are pure data; choose the class variant when descriptors need mutable/lazy internals or a framework requires a JavaBean.
pitfalls: Record equality is structural, so two separately loaded descriptors with the same components are equal yet are different entries in a registry - use ids as keys and never rely on descriptor equality.
The canonical constructor accepts anything: a data file with a negative base health or duplicate ids must be validated in a compact constructor or in the loader.
Records cannot hold any instance state beyond the header, so per-instance caches or derived counters belong on the typed object, not on the descriptor.
